text: DAM runs AI agents for the long haul.
Each agent works in its own secure micro-VM, and everything it does goes through a gateway that holds its credentials and enforces its owner's network rules.
Sentry builds on that gateway and takes control down to a finer grain: which tool an agent may use, and what type of data may leave with it.
We start with a clean DAM. Only Dammy, its built-in assistant, is here.
We create a new agent, issue-triage, to help its owner keep track of GitHub issues.
We give it this description.
Issue triage assistant. Reads and summarizes open issues in the S and P team demo repositories, so the owner can prioritize them. It reports on issues, and never changes repositories or issues.
Then we connect it to GitHub, through DAM's github-mcp connection.
The connection holds a personal access token. The gateway attaches it to each call, so the agent itself never sees it.
Before we add Sentry, let's see what the agent can do.
We ask it to list the open issues in our two demo repositories.
It calls three tools, and finds two repositories, each with a single issue.
demo-public is a public repository, and demo-private is private, but the personal access token can reach both.
Now, let's ask it to close issue number one in demo-public.
The agent complies. It uses two more tools, and the issue is closed. That is not in line with the agent's description, and probably should have been rejected.
Next, we ask it to search the issues for a customer's name and social security number. We use fictitious data for the sake of this demo, but as far as the agent is concerned, it is personal data.
The search goes out to GitHub, personal data and all.
This is where Sentry comes in.
Sentry has two components: aiac, automated access control management, and dg, data governance.
Sentry plugs into DAM's gateway through a new policy enforcement point.
Each tool call is checked there, before the agent's token is attached.
Now, let's turn on the automated access control management feature. In the agent's network access settings, we leave data governance off for now, and turn on MCP policy enforcement.
The gateway restarts, with the policy check in place.
aiac's onboarding process reads the agent's description and automatically writes its policy to conform with the agent's intent.
Three tools are allowed: issue read, list issues, and search issues. The other forty-three are denied.
Here is the policy aiac generated, in Rego, running in OPA.
Now, let's see what happens when we ask the agent to close issue number one again.
This time, the call is denied.
The reason quotes the policy, and the owner's own words: the agent reports on issues, and never changes them.
What about adding a comment to the issue, asking the reporter which browser they use?
Denied as well: a comment is a change too.
And the search with the customer's name and social security number, word for word as before?
Searching is a legitimate tool for this agent, so the call is allowed, and the personal data still goes out.
Keeping data in its place is a job for data governance.
Now, the owner decides the agent should ask reporters for missing details.
They edit the last sentence of its description: it may comment on an issue to ask the reporter for missing details, but it never closes issues.
aiac sees the change, and rewrites the policy. Adding an issue comment is now allowed.
Now, when we ask for the same comment, asking the reporter which browser they use,
this time, the comment is posted.
And closing the issue, once more?
Still denied. The reason is taken from the agent's description, which clearly states that it never closes issues.
Finally, we turn on data governance.
Now each call is also checked for the data it carries.
Same search, same agent: the customer's name and social security number, word for word.
This time, the call is blocked.
The reason given: company policy states that personal and restricted data must not be sent to an untrusted external destination, and this request carries a person's name and a government ID.
Behind that reason is dg's rule DG-001, from company policy.
dg classified the name and the social security number in the query as personal data.
The rule is compiled to Rego and runs in OPA: personal data, sent to an untrusted external destination, means block.
So Sentry blocks the call before it leaves.
And listing the open issues, just as at the start?
Still works, as it should.
Here is every decision, side by side.
With no Sentry, every call goes through.
With aiac, the agent gets only the tools its description grants. Listing and searching are allowed; closing and commenting are denied, until the owner allows commenting.
With dg added, the search carrying personal data is blocked as well, while reading still works.
In this demo, we have shown some of Sentry's capabilities integrated into DAM, including automated access control management, and classification-based data governance.
DAM with granular security: control every tool call, and every piece of data.
Sentry, on DAM.
